title: Dan Richards Tells Joe Rogan Archaeology Is a Faith, Not a Science, and the Pacific Northwest Held 3,000 Elongated Skulls

content:
Dan Richards, a researcher and YouTube creator focused on alternative archaeology, returned to the Joe Rogan Experience to argue that the human past is far stranger and more suppressed than mainstream institutions admit. Richards claims that artificial cranial deformation was a global, status-driven practice, with the largest known concentration—3,000 burials—once visible at Mount Coffin in Washington State, not in Peru. He links elongated skulls, polydactyly, and cleft palates to genetic admixture between Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, and Denisovans, suggesting ancient South American cultures may have deliberately bred for these traits. His broader critique is methodological: archaeology, he says, cannot replicate its findings and therefore functions more like a church than a lab, with institutions from the Smithsonian to the Rockefeller family accused of hiding anomalous remains. Rogan plays the skeptic, countering that the most mundane explanation—private collectors buying artifacts on a $3 billion black market—is probably the truth. The episode concludes with both men promoting a conference in Austin, leaving unresolved whether the past is being suppressed or simply sold.

A Battle Over Who Owns the Human Past

The claim that most people missed from Dan Richards' appearance on the Joe Rogan Experience is not about Peru. It is about a place called Mount Coffin in Longview, Washington. Richards, an alternative archaeology researcher, says an American naval officer in the 19th century saw 3,000 above-ground burials there, and that all of them contained elongated skulls. If true, that single site would represent the largest concentration of deliberately deformed human skulls ever recorded in modern history. The site was later burned, mined by a cement company, and paved into a pyramid-shaped town plan. Almost nothing remains to verify it.

That is the pattern Richards returned to for nearly three hours: the most important evidence keeps vanishing, and the people who could prove it either will not release the material or no longer have it. Richards frames this as institutional suppression. Rogan, the host, repeatedly pushes back with a simpler explanation—money. Private collectors paid for the best artifacts before museums could catalog them, and a black market worth roughly $3 billion a year encourages people to keep quiet. The result is a dispute that is less about skulls than about who gets to decide what happened 12,000 years ago.

The Chinook Sign of Freedom

Richards opened his argument by handing Rogan a Smithsonian pamphlet titled The Chinook Sign of Freedom. The title is the argument. When Lewis and Clark crossed the Cascade Mountains and reached the Columbia River, Richards says every Native American group west of the Cascades practiced artificial cranial modification. The deformed skull was not a mark of isolation or illness—it was proof you were not a slave. "If you didn't have an artificially modified skull, you were a slave," he said.

The pamphlet itself is real, and so is the practice it documents. The Chinook Sign of Freedom is a 20-page study published by the Smithsonian Institution in 1960, in which the physical anthropologist Thomas Dale Stewart examined the skull of Chief Concomly. The Oregon Historical Society records head flattening as "a mark of status among the Chinookan people," begun at birth and continued for eight to twelve months until the forehead was permanently reshaped; among the Chinook, only slaves and outsiders went without it. William Clark sketched the cradle boards used to produce the effect in his journal in 1806, and the artist Paul Kane, traveling the Columbia in the 1840s, found that Chinookans looked with disdain on "round heads," whether white or Indian. The custom had faded by the end of the nineteenth century; as late as the 1950s, a resident of Celilo Village was thought to be the last living Columbia River Indian with a flattened head.

▲ Two artificially deformed crania, recorded as from the Columbia River region, from a historical medical collection. The elongation was produced by binding in infancy. (Image: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0)

The pivotal figure is Chief Concomly, a Chinook leader who met Lewis and Clark and who, Richards claims, attributed his intellect to his elongated skull. Concomly married his daughters to fur trappers and advised against attacking white settlers, pointing to their woven cloth and firearms. He died in 1830, during an intermittent fever epidemic that swept the lower Columbia. Five years later a Hudson's Bay Company physician, Meredith Gairdner, took the skull from his grave and sent it to Britain. It was displayed for more than a century at the Royal Naval Hospital Haslar, where it was damaged in the Blitz, before returning to the United States in 1953, passing to the Smithsonian in 1956, and being repatriated to Chinook tribal members for reburial in 1972. Richards says it emerged five years after the repatriation that someone had engraved the back of the skull.

The scale of the phenomenon is the load-bearing claim. Richards cites Mount Coffin, where Lieutenant Charles Wilkes—whose father, Richards notes, was a member of the Skull and Bones Society in England—reported the 3,000 burials. Richards reasons that because only nobles could be buried there, and nobility required modification, the arithmetic is simple. "3,000 elongated skulls. Not complicated here," he said. A campfire burned the site; local histories date the fire to August 1841, when Wilkes's party was using the rock to make astronomical observations for the U.S. Exploring Expedition. The Portland Star and Cement Company bought the mountain and mined it away, and in 1929 the rock was dynamited and quarried down for gravel used in building the Port of Longview. The Daughters of the American Revolution tried to buy it and failed. Longview was then laid out on a pyramid floor plan, its four main arcs paved with gravel from the mountain.

Richards did not stop at Washington. He claims an older peer-reviewed map of artificial cranial deformation contains more information than a newer one, with areas erased—including the island of Newi and ancient Hawaii, where he says 8.9% of excavated skulls were elongated.

The Archaic Brain Case Theory

The most mechanistic argument Richards offered is that cranial modification was not purely cosmetic. He links elongated skulls to Chiari malformation type 1, a condition where the base of the cerebellum pushes down into the spinal cord, causing migraines and other symptoms. Recent science, he says, suggests the condition may stem from Neanderthal and Denisovan brain cases not fitting properly within a modern human skull. His inference: if a population suffered chronic cranial pressure, elongating the back of the skull each generation—or drilling holes through trepanation—would relieve it.

He supports this with Neanderthal anatomy. The Neanderthal brain case, he notes, is wider at the back, where motor skills, smell, sight, and hearing are processed, while the frontal lobe—associated with decision-making—is smaller than in modern humans. Rogan and Richards agree this suggests formidable athletic and sensory capacity paired with different cognitive strengths.

The genetic thread runs through several conditions Richards says cluster together.

TraitClaimed associationWhere Richards says it clusters
Elongated skullsStatus marker, possible pressure reliefPacific Northwest, Paracas, Easter Island, China
Polydactyly (6 fingers/toes)GLI3 variant in Neanderthal/Denisovan DNAPeru, Brazil, biblical giant accounts
Cleft palate / "jaguar" featuresArchaic admixtureMoche jaguar people, trophy skulls
Wormian "Inca bones"Skull-plate stress, lack of equilibriumInca territory, Easter Island, Asia
Chiari malformation type 1Brain-skull size mismatchPresent-day clinical cases

The boldest inference is that South American cultures were deliberately mingling bloodlines. Rogan supplied the hypothetical framework, asking what would happen if a Neanderthal and a Homo sapiens met, solved a problem together, and "walk away from that with mad respect for the other person's ability to see what they don't. Wouldn't they want to mingle that?" Richards says Paracas was the last place still doing it, an evolutionary arms race combining one species' intelligence with the other's sensory capacity. When Rogan noted that you would expect to see larger-headed populations in Peru today, Richards attributed the absence to the practice becoming illegal and natural selection against extreme cases.

Archaeology as a Church

Richards' most portable argument is not about skulls but about method. His test for science is replicability. "If I combine hydrogen and oxygen and you combine hydrogen, we should get the same thing. Now, if I dig up something in my backyard, can you replicate that?" By that standard, he places archaeology alongside theology—a discipline whose core findings are one-off and unrepeatable. Archaeologists, he concedes, do call in physicists to carbon date and maintain chains of custody on construction sites. But the discipline's central claims, he argues, cannot be tested the way astronomy can, where a hundred telescopes can train on the same supernova.

He extends this to the Clovis-first paradigm, the idea that humans entered the Americas around 13,000 years ago with the Clovis culture. Richards cites the Folsom tradition's Wikipedia page, which he says still records that any archaeologist desirous of a successful career could not posit an earlier peopling of the Americas without two men destroying their career. He then turns to the Society for American Archaeology's original bylaws, which he says committed the society to cultivating a better relationship between interested amateurs and professionals. "They now do neither," he said.

Rogan supplies the motive: ego and money. Amateur researchers like Jimmy Corsetti, Luke Caverns, and Ben Van Kerkwyk can film anywhere and attract millions of views. Academics need funding, approvals, and tenure. Richards describes the Society's letter to Netflix about Graham Hancock's show, which he says listed three problems. The first, he claims, was not factual error but that Hancock "talks shit about archaeologists and doesn't listen to us." The third was that the show promotes white supremacy—a charge Richards rebuts by noting that Ignatius Donnelly, the 1882 writer the letter blames, was an abolitionist and feminist. Two earlier French-American writers who cast the Maya as Atlantean conquerors, Richards says, are ignored because they don't fit the narrative.

Richards' prescription is engagement, not dismissal. He describes Corsetti posting on X that the biblical Nephilim might be Denisovan or Neanderthal; archaeologists mocked him because both species were thought shorter than humans. Richards let the pile-on run, then suggested Corsetti look into Gigantopithecus instead. "You take somebody's passion, they're looking at the rabbit hole, you shove them in head first. That's science communication."

The Disappearing Evidence

The cover-up claims are specific and repeated. Richards traces the Rockefeller family's involvement to the 1930s, when Peruvian archaeologist Julio Tello announced elongated skulls at Paracas while working on roughly $300 a year. A Rockefeller, he says, made an unexpected trip to Peru, paid $3,000 for four grave bundles—ten times Tello's annual stipend, out of about 300 bundles—and returned to New York. The four bundles were supposedly displayed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the American Museum of Natural History. Richards says no photographs or drawings exist, and whether they were repatriated depends on whom you ask.

He applies the same logic to a 1909 newspaper story about explorer G.E. Kincaid finding a cave citadel in the Grand Canyon with mummies, copper and gold vessels, hieroglyphs, and space for 50,000 inhabitants. Richards acknowledges the story is regarded as a hoax, but his objection is that the area remains restricted. Rogan counters that a genuine discovery of that scale would make its finder famous. Richards responds that a mainstream archaeologist who contradicts the gatekeepers risks their job, citing a colleague who retracted statements after pressure from Flint Dibble.

The giant-skeleton thread follows the same pattern. Richards names Aleš Hrdlička, a Bohemia-born physician who left medicine for anthropology and became the Smithsonian's curator of physical anthropology—a collector of human remains whose gathering of specimens to support racist beliefs was documented by a Washington Post investigation in 2023. Hrdlička dismissed reports of giant Native American bones in 1934 by accusing earlier researchers of mismeasuring. Richards calls this a vested interest dressed as rigor. He cites a 1959 case in which Dr. Don Dragoo of the Carnegie Museum measured a skeleton in an Adena mound and said it indicated a person 7 feet 3 inches tall in life. Dragoo was dismissed on the grounds that he had only taken an in-ground measurement. The skeleton cannot now be located.

Richards also describes redactions in peer-reviewed papers on the Hueco Tanks and Gila Cliff Dwellings in the Southwest, where artifact descriptions appear as blacked-out bars. His most mundane explanation is the one he favors: people are selling what they find. "If it's a giant bone or an elongated skull and you want to know more about it, real good chance you're not going to be able to find anything."

Mummy Powder and a $3 Billion Black Market

The episode's grimmest material concerned the consumption of human remains as medicine. From roughly the 12th to the 18th century, ground mummy—"mummy powder"—was sold as medicine across Europe. Demand was high enough that forgers began manufacturing fake mummies when supply ran short. By the 19th century the pretense had collapsed into entertainment: in 1834, surgeon Thomas Pettigrew unwrapped a mummy at the Royal College of Surgeons, and wealthy hosts staged unwrapping parties with strong drink and appreciative audiences. Richards notes the "curse" narrative that followed, including the sudden death of Lord Carnarvon after Tutankhamun's tomb was opened.

Richards and Rogan then browsed dealer sites selling antiquities. Items discussed include a Peruvian mask listed at $4,850, an Egyptian bronze cobra dated 664–30 BCE, a gold standing shaman pendant that is 89% gold and weighs 148 grams, and a gold wing deity pendant at $67,000. The shaman figure drew attention for its seven or eight fingers and the heads it appears to hold. Richards notes that provenance matters legally—artifacts acquired after a certain date cannot be sold—and compares the regime to pre-ban ivory.

Trophy skulls are described as drilled and hung from belts, with one example said to be the only known trophy skull with a cleft lip. Richards says the Spanish recorded that people born with cleft lips were placed in temples as holy workers, and that six fingers and deformations were likewise considered holy.

The Candelabra and the Genetic Engineering Hypothesis

Richards' most speculative argument concerns the Paracas Candelabra, a geoglyph visible 12 miles out to sea. He compares its three-pronged fork shape to a family tree diagram and proposes it as a marker for where bloodlines were mingled. He says the same forked symbol appears carved on two Easter Island skulls, one of which he calls a bird man. Rogan asked directly whether Richards drew the genetic-engineering conclusion from the image; Richards said no—the image is "the icing on the cake," and the real evidence is genetic papers linking deformations to Denisovan and Neanderthal admixture.

He supports the contact thesis with genetics, claiming there is genetic drift in both directions between Easter Island and Peru. He invokes the Polynesian concept of a world navel—Cusco, Jerusalem's Western Wall, and Delphi are examples—and notes that Easter Island has one despite being far-flung, which he says makes sense if lower sea levels made it the center of a string of islands. He calls Easter Island the place with the most remaining to find because it has been dug and looted far less than Rome or Egypt.

On ancient aliens, Richards is explicit about his priors. He tells a story about David Childress: if you left the room and your wallet vanished, you could blame a dog or an alien, but you would suspect Childress. "That doesn't mean there's no aliens and doesn't mean there's no dogs. Just means that we all know what's most likely." Richards says he is not opposed to the idea but needs to be convinced. Rogan notes that if humans were genetically engineered, Peru would be the best candidate site, and Richards agrees the hypothesis is not absurd given that humans already genetically engineer animals.

Where the Two Hosts Disagree

For all the agreement, Rogan's counterweights mark the limits. He argues that archaeology does maintain chains of custody on construction finds in Mexico City, and that the most mundane explanation for redactions—someone selling artifacts—is probably correct. Richards agrees on that last point. "The best of the best always gone," Rogan said, framing the pattern of elite artifacts vanishing into private collections rather than staying in public museums.

Where they diverge most is on ancient aliens, which Rogan treats as the least likely explanation and Richards treats as unfalsifiable but unpersuasive. The episode's unresolved tension is the one Richards himself names: he cannot verify the strongest claims, and the institutions that could verify them will not release the material. Whether that reflects suppression or simply the ordinary difficulty of doing science on unique, unrepeatable finds is the question neither host settles.

The closing discussion turned to the conference both men are promoting: the Quest for Ancient Civilizations, October 16–18, 2026, at ACL Live in Austin, with Randall Carlson, Billy Carson, Kurt Metzger, Duncan Trussell, David Childress, and Georges St-Pierre. Richards says he has refused AI clipping, AI thumbnails, and AI communication with his audience—a stance he says caused at least one production team to walk away.

The concrete items to watch are the Paracas skull measurements, the disputed Carnegie Museum skeleton, the restricted Grand Canyon area, and whether the genetic papers Richards cites on archaic admixture and polydactyly accumulate into a coherent case. The debate over the human past is not going away. The only question is whether the evidence is being suppressed or simply sold to the highest bidder.
